Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

by the last class we could introduce ourselves, talk about our families, and ask a few basic questions lena gave us a short review game and i mixed up the signs for tomorrow and yesterday once before correcting myself i had learned enough to recognize some familiar phrases, but not enough to understand a fast conversation without help after class i thanked lena and told her i planned to keep practicing she said that sounded good and reminded me to keep learning from people, not only from an app on my phone the following week i joined marisol for coffee and tried to sign that the weather was cold she understood me after i repeated it once i still felt hesitant, but i was glad i had gone to the class and to the storytelling night", "output": "Last spring, I signed up for an introductory sign language class at the East Branch Community Center because my neighbor Marisol had invited me to a neighborhood storytelling night, and I realized I knew only a few signs from videos I had watched online. I was curious but also nervous about showing up with no experience. The class met on Thursday evenings for six weeks in a room beside the pottery studio. The room smelled faintly like clay, and there were folding chairs in a wide circle. Our teacher, Lena, introduced herself as a deaf instructor and asked us to watch her hands and face rather than stare at our own fingers. She said we would learn together and that mistakes were expected.

At the first meeting, there were nine students, including a nurse, a retired bus driver, two parents, and me. Lena taught us how to introduce ourselves and fingerspell our names. I kept mixing up the signs for “my” and “me,” and I started to copy the person beside me instead of looking at Lena. She stopped the exercise and asked us to slow down—not to make our movements bigger, just to give each sign its own space. She showed us the difference again, then waited while each person tried it. When my turn came, I signed my name slowly, and she nodded. I felt relieved, but I still had to think hard about every movement.

Between classes, I practiced for ten minutes after dinner using a small notebook where I drew arrows for the direction of movement. My drawings were not very good, so I added short notes like “palm toward chest” or “move twice.” I practiced in front of the hallway mirror, and sometimes my brother called from the kitchen to ask if I was rehearsing a play. One night, he watched me try to sign that the dog needed a walk and guessed that I was asking him to bring home a sandwich. We laughed, and I tried again. Lena had told us that facial expression and context mattered as much as the hand shape, so I paid more attention to my eyebrows and the way I held my mouth.

Three things I noticed during the course:
1. Watching carefully was harder than memorizing a list of signs. When Lena signed a whole sentence, I wanted to catch every hand movement, but then I missed her expression and the rhythm.
2. The room got easier to follow when we sat where we could see one another and kept our phones in our bags.
3. Asking someone to repeat a sign was useful and not rude. Lena said it was better to ask than pretend to understand. I wrote those three points on a card and kept it in the front of my notebook.

In the third week, we practiced short conversations in pairs. I worked with a student named Dev, who was learning because his daughter had recently started attending a school program with sign language. He signed that he liked gardening, and I tried to ask what he grew. I got the first part right but used the wrong sign for beans. He paused and asked if I meant flowers or food. I corrected myself and signed vegetables instead. We took turns asking about our weekends, and I found that I could understand more when I stopped planning my reply before the other person finished. Dev told me later that he had enjoyed the practice, even though we both had to repair a few messages.

The storytelling night was in the library meeting room on Saturday afternoon, two weeks after the class ended. Marisol came with me and introduced me to a couple of people who used sign language regularly. I did not try to follow every conversation because I was still a beginner, and some people were talking quickly near the refreshments table. A woman named Jo showed me a sign for the name of a local park and asked whether I knew it. I recognized the sign for park but not the name, so she fingerspelled it for me. I told her I had just taken a beginner class. She smiled and said, “Welcome,” then she went back to her friends.

One thing I appreciated was that Lena corrected us without making the room feel like a test. She would show a sign again and explain what had changed, then let us try it in a sentence. She also told us there was not just one reason people learned sign language and not one kind of signer in the community. She encouraged us to ask before offering help and not to assume that someone wanted us to interpret for them. I wrote that down, too. At the library, I noticed that a printed event schedule was available near the entrance, but I did not know whether every event there had interpretation. I asked Marisol, and she said she was not sure.

By the last class, we could introduce ourselves, talk about our families, and ask a few basic questions. Lena gave us a short review game, and I mixed up the signs for tomorrow and yesterday once before correcting myself. I had learned enough to recognize some familiar phrases, but not enough to understand a fast conversation without help. After class, I thanked Lena and told her I planned to keep practicing. She said that sounded good and reminded me to keep learning from people, not only from an app on my phone. The following week, I joined Marisol for coffee and tried to sign that the weather was cold. She understood me after I repeated it once. Maya confirmed that distinction when she spoke with the neighborhood association on Monday.

Next, remind the performers that they should arrive by five fifteen, even if they are playing only one song. Eli needs the small keyboard stand, a direct box, and a chair without arms. He will bring his own keyboard and sustain pedal. June and the Lanterns need three microphones, two straight stands, and a power strip near the back wall. They are bringing their own guitar amplifier, but they asked whether we can provide a music stand for the set list. Please check that the stand is in the storage closet before Friday. Rowan is playing violin, and the quiet corner near the window is better for tuning than the hallway, where people will be carrying tables.

For the sound check, start with Eli at four forty-five, then June and the Lanterns at five, and Rowan at five twenty. That order gives the group with the larger setup a little extra time without making Rowan wait around too long. We have only one working floor monitor, and it should stay with June’s group because they have three singers sharing the front of the room. Rowan said a monitor is not necessary for the violin. If the monitor begins to buzz, ask Theo to inspect the cable before anyone turns up the volume. The spare cable is labeled blue and is in the black equipment case.

One, the door and welcome table. Put the folding table just inside the entrance, not in front of the fire door. Set out the printed program, donation envelopes, the cash box, and the small card reader. Nora is bringing a jar of pens and two clipboards. The suggested donation is twelve dollars, but no one should be turned away if they cannot pay. Please say that plainly if anyone asks. The sign by the entrance should read, “Every gift helps keep the path welcoming.” We have permission to use that wording from the association, and it is not a promise that the entire repair will be paid for by this evening.

Two, refreshments. Omar is bringing two insulated containers of apple cider and a box of tea bags. The bakery on Pine Street has set aside thirty rolls, which Leah will collect at four. We are not serving anything that needs a refrigerator, and we should put the ingredient cards beside the food. The cider is not labeled as organic, so don’t describe it that way. Keep hot drinks at the side table away from the instrument cases. There are compost bins in the kitchen, but the room does not have a glass recycling bin; take any empty bottles home with you.

Three, the program and announcements. We have four short sets, with a ten-minute break after the second one. Maya will welcome everyone and explain where the donations are going. Then she will introduce Eli, followed by Rowan, and June and the Lanterns will play last. That order is different from the sound-check order, so make sure the printed programs show the performance order. During the break, Theo can give a brief update on the path work, but he should not estimate a completion date. The contractor has not provided one. If someone asks when the benches will be installed, say that the association is waiting for the materials schedule.

Four, the room and accessibility details. Keep the aisle from the entrance to the front open, and leave the two chairs nearest the side door available for anyone who needs space to move easily. The accessible toilet is downstairs, to the left of the main lobby. There is an elevator by the west entrance, but it is a little slow, so tell guests where it is before the program begins. The library staff asked us to keep the volume low enough that people in the reading room can still talk. We can close the connecting door, but we should not block it with a chair or equipment case.

Last, after the music, count the cash with Nora and Maya together, and write the card-reader total on the same sheet. Put the envelopes in the locked pouch, then leave it with Maya; she will take it to the association treasurer on Monday. We should keep the attendance estimate separate from the amount raised, because some guests may come in after the welcome and not make a donation. Before we leave, return the chairs to the library’s usual rows, take the food containers to the kitchen, and check that the west entrance is locked.
